content: Who has believed our message? To whom has the LORD’s arm been revealed? {{v:2}} For he grew up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of dry ground. He has no good looks or majesty. When we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him. {{v:3}} He was despised and rejected by men, a man of suffering and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. {{v:4}} Surely he has borne our sickness and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. {{v:5}} But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. {{v:6}} All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all. {{v:7}} He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he didn’t open his mouth. {{v:8}} He was taken away by oppression and judgment. As for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people? {{v:9}} They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence, nor was any deceit in his mouth. {{v:10}} Yet it pleased the LORD to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he will see his offspring. He will prolong his days and the LORD’s pleasure will prosper in his hand. {{v:11}} After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. {{v:12}} Therefore I will give him a portion with the great. He will divide the plunder with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was counted with the transgressors; yet he bore the sins of many and made intercession for the transgressors.

facets.evidence: he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
facets.text: Isaiah's fourth Servant Song portrays a servant whose suffering is not incidental but vicarious and substitutionary: 'he was pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities.' The punishment that produces our peace falls on him, and by his wounds we are healed. The passage teaches that one innocent sufferer bears the guilt that belongs to the many, so that redemption comes through his affliction rather than in spite of it.
facets.question: What does Isaiah 53 mean when it says the servant was pierced for our transgressions?

facets.evidence: NT fulfillment pattern: Acts 8:32-35 cites this passage explicitly; patristic and magisterial consensus reads the Suffering Servant as prophecy of Christ's passion; the silent lamb and wounds correspond to Gospel details.
facets.text: The Church reads this Suffering Servant as a direct prophecy of Jesus Christ's passion, fulfilled in the Gospels and cited by Philip to the Ethiopian eunuch in Acts 8:32-35. The silent lamb led to slaughter is fulfilled in Christ's silence before Pilate and Herod, and the servant's stripes become the wounds of the crucified Lord. Thus Isaiah announces the mystery of the cross centuries before Calvary.
facets.question: How is the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53 fulfilled in Jesus Christ?

facets.evidence: NT citation: John 1:29 and Revelation's Lamb Once Slain; the passage's own words 'as a lamb that is led to the slaughter... so he didn't open his mouth' provide the image; tradition universally connects this sacrificial silence to Christ's atonement.
facets.text: The servant is described as 'a lamb that is led to the slaughter' who did not open his mouth, uniting the sacrificial imagery of the Passover lamb with a willing, uncomplaining victim. This grounds the New Testament proclamation of Christ as 'the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world' (John 1:29) and the Lamb once slain in Revelation. The image reveals that atonement is offered in meekness and free obedience, not in violent resistance.
facets.question: Why is the Suffering Servant portrayed as a silent lamb led to slaughter?

facets.evidence: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
facets.text: The passage confesses collective human waywardness in a striking image: 'All we like sheep have gone astray; everyone has turned to his own way.' Sin here is not merely individual failing but a shared straying of the whole flock, each pursuing his own path. Against this scattering, the LORD lays the iniquity of all upon the one servant, gathering the guilt of the many onto a single bearer.
facets.question: What does it mean that we have all gone astray like sheep in Isaiah 53?

facets.evidence: Evident arc of the passage: the servant's rejection stems from having 'no good looks or majesty... no beauty that we should desire him,' and the onlookers' misreading is stated as 'we considered him plagued, struck by God'; the theological inference that God's saving work is hidden in what the world scorns follows directly from these contrasted statements.
facets.text: The servant is rejected precisely because he lacks worldly appeal: 'no good looks or majesty... no beauty that we should desire him,' despised and hidden from. The passage teaches that God's saving work comes disguised in what the world scorns, and that human judgment misreads suffering as divine punishment ('we considered him plagued, struck by God'). Faith must therefore look past appearances to recognize the hidden glory of redemptive suffering.
facets.question: Why does the world despise and misjudge the Suffering Servant?

facets.evidence: Inference from servant's post-suffering vindication ('he will see the light and be satisfied,' 'prolong his days') to resurrection: the text speaks of future life after death but does not use the word resurrection or explicitly identify this with Christ's rising.
facets.text: The passage moves from humiliation to exaltation: after making his soul 'an offering for sin,' the servant 'will see the light and be satisfied,' prolong his days, and see his offspring. This foreshadows the resurrection, in which Christ's self-offering is vindicated and made fruitful in a multitude of the redeemed. The servant's death is not the end but the seed of a new and enduring people.
facets.question: How does Isaiah 53 point toward the servant's vindication and resurrection?

facets.evidence: NT and Pauline connection: the passage's own words 'my righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities' are read by the tradition as the seedbed of justification theology; Romans 5 and Pauline soteriology cite this servant pattern as fulfilled in Christ.
facets.text: The servant 'will justify many by the knowledge of himself' and 'bear their iniquities,' introducing the language of justification through the servant's atoning work. It is not the many who make themselves righteous, but the righteous servant who confers righteousness by taking their sins upon himself. This anticipates the Pauline theology of justification by Christ's redemptive death.
facets.question: How does the servant justify the many in Isaiah 53?

facets.evidence: Traditional fulfillment reading: Gospel details of Christ crucified between criminals and buried in Joseph of Arimathea's tomb are universally read by the tradition as fulfilling 'they made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death.'
facets.text: The passage notes puzzling details of the servant's burial: 'they made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death,' though he was guiltless of violence or deceit. The tradition sees this fulfilled in Christ crucified between criminals yet buried in the tomb of the wealthy Joseph of Arimathea. The precision of the prophecy underscores that even the servant's death and burial unfold according to God's foreknown plan.
facets.question: What is the meaning of the servant being buried with the wicked and a rich man?

facets.evidence: NT link to Christ's eternal priesthood (Hebrews 7:25, Romans 8:34) and the passage's own words 'he poured out his soul to death and was counted with the transgressors… and made intercession for the transgressors' together establish the servant as both sacrificial victim and mediator, a connection the tradition affirms without argument.
facets.text: The passage culminates in the servant's priestly intercession: he 'poured out his soul to death and was counted with the transgressors, yet he bore the sins of many and made intercession for the transgressors.' By numbering himself among sinners and pleading on their behalf, the servant acts as both victim and mediator. This unites his sacrifice with his ongoing prayer for those he redeems, a foreshadowing of Christ's eternal priesthood.
facets.question: How does the Suffering Servant intercede for transgressors?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Isaiah 53, the fourth Servant Song, presents the Suffering Servant as an innocent figure who bears vicarious, substitutionary punishment for the sins of the many, healing them through his wounds; the Church reads this passage as the preeminent Old Testament prophecy of Christ's passion, atoning death, and vindication.

[scriptural/doctrinal | explicit]: The servant's affliction is not random but purposefully substitutionary — he takes upon himself the transgressions and iniquities of others so that those guilty parties receive peace and healing. One wholly innocent figure absorbs the penalty owed by the many, making redemption inseparable from his voluntary suffering.

[typological/scriptural | settled]: Christian tradition and the New Testament — notably Philip's catechesis in Acts 8 — identify this passage as direct prophetic anticipation of Jesus Christ's passion, fulfilled in his silent endurance before Pilate and Herod and in the wounds of his crucifixion. Centuries before Calvary, Isaiah discloses the mystery of the cross.

[typological/doctrinal | settled]: The servant's portrayal as a voiceless lamb led to slaughter draws on Passover sacrificial imagery, linking a willing and obedient victim to the New Testament proclamation of Christ as Lamb of God (John 1:29) and the slain Lamb of Revelation. Atonement is thus shown to operate through meekness and free self-offering rather than resistance.

[scriptural/doctrinal | explicit]: The confession "all we like sheep have gone astray" frames sin as a universal, collective wandering — not merely isolated personal failure but a shared dispersal of the entire human flock. In response, the LORD concentrates the guilt of the scattered many onto the single servant, who gathers and bears what all have incurred.

[scriptural/devotional | settled]: The servant's lack of outward splendor — no majesty, no desirable appearance — and his rejection by onlookers who mistake his suffering for divine punishment demonstrate that God's salvific action is often hidden beneath what the world scorns. Authentic faith must pierce through appearances to recognize glory concealed within redemptive humiliation.

[typological/doctrinal | inferential]: After his self-offering, the servant is promised prolonged days, spiritual offspring, and satisfied sight of light — imagery that foreshadows the resurrection, where Christ's death becomes the seed of a redeemed community. The servant's humiliation is not a terminus but the generative source of an enduring new people.

[typological/doctrinal | settled]: The servant "justifies many" by bearing their iniquities himself, so that righteousness is conferred from outside rather than achieved from within. This servant-mediated justification through atoning death anticipates the Pauline doctrine of justification by Christ's redemptive work, where the righteous one imparts what sinners cannot earn.

[typological/scriptural | settled]: The detail that the servant's grave was placed with the wicked yet also with a wealthy man, despite his personal innocence, is seen as fulfilled in Christ crucified between criminals and buried in Joseph of Arimathea's tomb. The prophetic precision of these burial circumstances confirms that every stage of the servant's death unfolds within God's foreknown plan.

[typological/doctrinal | settled]: The servant who "poured out his soul to death" and was numbered among transgressors simultaneously "made intercession" for them, uniting the roles of sacrificial victim and priestly mediator. This dual function — self-oblation joined to ongoing intercession — foreshadows Christ's eternal high-priesthood, in which his once-for-all sacrifice and his perpetual advocacy for the redeemed are inseparable.
